name: William Morales
description: William "Guillermo" Morales (b. 1950) was a leading bomb-maker for the FALN, the clandestine Puerto Rican independence group. On July 12, 1978 a device exploded in his Queens, New York apartment, blowing off both of his hands and disfiguring his face. Convicted on weapons and explosives charges, he made a dramatic escape from the Bellevue Hospital prison ward in May 1979, fled to Mexico (where he was imprisoned after a 1983 shootout), and was eventually granted political asylum in Cuba, where he still lives in exile.

cases.charges: Possession of weapons and explosives (FALN bomb factory, Queens, July 12, 1978)
cases.sentence: Roughly ten years; escaped from the Bellevue Hospital prison ward on May 21, 1979, later imprisoned in Mexico (1983–1988), then granted political asylum in Cuba

name: Carlos Feliciano
description: Carlos Feliciano was a veteran Puerto Rican independence militant arrested in New York in May 1970 and accused of a campaign of bombings. Defended by attorney William Kunstler, his supporters denounced the case as a frame-up; after a 1971 trial ended in a hung jury he was retried, convicted only on a lesser possession charge, and freed in 1973.

cases.charges: Possession of explosives / alleged bombing campaign (denounced by his defense as a frame-up)
cases.convicted: Convicted on a possession charge after a 1971 mistrial
cases.sentence: Held roughly three years; released in 1973

name: Eduardo Cruz
description: Eduardo "Pancho" Cruz was a young Puerto Rican independence activist who became the subject of a 1972 defense campaign — the Eduardo Cruz Defense Committee and the pamphlet "Repression and Colonization: The Case of Eduardo 'Pancho' Cruz" — which described him as framed and convicted and called for his freedom. Specifics of the charge and sentence are not well documented.

cases.charges: Framed and convicted (per the Eduardo Cruz Defense Committee, 1972); specific charge not documented

name: Juan Otero
description: Juan Otero (Juan Otero Jr.) was a South Bronx Puerto Rican community activist and construction-trades anti-discrimination organizer — a family man, educational specialist, and young father with no prior police record — who led pickets against discriminatory hiring at New York building sites. On March 20, 1973 he was convicted after a jury trial in Bronx County, on consolidated indictments, of burglary in the second and third degrees, two counts of grand larceny in the third degree, and attempted grand larceny, and sentenced to concurrent indeterminate terms of up to five years. A defense campaign — the Committee to Defend Juan Otero and a Puerto Rican Socialist Party statement carried in Workers World — held that he had been framed on the burglary charges by "vengeful Bronx cops" and racist building-trades interests in retaliation for his organizing. On September 26, 1974 the Appellate Division unanimously reversed his conviction and ordered a new trial (People v. Otero, 45 A.D.2d 952, 359 N.Y.S.2d 318): his defense was alibi, the conviction rested entirely on identification testimony whose conflicting character "casts considerable doubt" on the charges, and the court found improper bolstering of that eyewitness identification. His exact arrest and release dates are not documented; he was imprisoned during 1973, with a possible maximum documented custody of March 20, 1973 – September 26, 1974 (about 555 days) if held continuously.

cases.charges: Burglary in the second and third degrees, two counts of grand larceny in the third degree, and attempted grand larceny (consolidated indictments, jury trial, Bronx County) — which the "Free Juan Otero" campaign and a Puerto Rican Socialist Party statement called a frame-up by Bronx police and building-trades interests in retaliation for his anti-discrimination organizing.
cases.convicted: Convicted March 20, 1973 (jury, Bronx County); conviction unanimously reversed and a new trial ordered September 26, 1974 — People v. Otero, 45 A.D.2d 952, 359 N.Y.S.2d 318 (identification testimony "casts considerable doubt"; improper bolstering of eyewitness ID).
cases.sentence: Concurrent indeterminate terms of up to five years (up to 5 years on each burglary count, up to 4 years on each grand-larceny count; unconditional discharge on the attempt). Actual time served not documented — possible maximum custody March 20, 1973 – September 26, 1974 (~555 days).

name: José "Cha Cha" Jiménez
description: José "Cha Cha" Jiménez founded the Young Lords in Chicago, transforming a Puerto Rican street gang into a revolutionary political organization and a member of Fred Hampton's original Rainbow Coalition. He was arrested and jailed repeatedly as an organizer, and the group's political awakening began during his incarceration.

cases.charges: Repeated arrests as a Young Lords organizer in Chicago (late 1960s–1970s)

name: Tom Dostou
description: Tom Dostou was a field marshal of the Patriot Party, the organization of anti-racist working-class white people that was part of Fred Hampton's original Rainbow Coalition alongside the Black Panther Party and the Young Lords. He was arrested in February 1970 when police raided the party's offices and detained its leadership.

cases.charges: Arrested in a February 1970 police raid on the Patriot Party offices

name: Chuck Armsbury
description: Chuck Armsbury chaired the Eugene, Oregon chapter of the Patriot Party, the white working-class wing of the Rainbow Coalition that organized alongside the Black Panther Party. He spent years in federal prison on charges his supporters called trumped-up, and while imprisoned at McNeil Island Federal Penitentiary co-filed a 1970 prisoners' "Genocide Complaint" against the federal government.

cases.charges: Federal charges (denounced by supporters as trumped-up political prosecution)

name: Bobby Rush
description: Bobby Rush co-founded the Illinois chapter of the Black Panther Party with Fred Hampton in 1968 and survived the COINTELPRO campaign that killed Hampton. He served six months in 1972 on a weapons charge and later became a Chicago alderman and, for three decades, a U.S. Congressman.

name: Pablo "Yoruba" Guzmán
description: Pablo "Yoruba" Guzmán was Minister of Information of the New York Young Lords and was arrested in the group's 1969–70 direct actions, including the occupation of the First Spanish Methodist Church in East Harlem and the takeover of Lincoln Hospital. He later became an Emmy-winning New York broadcast journalist.

cases.charges: Arrests in Young Lords direct actions (New York City, 1969–70)
